examDifficulty.heading: Is the Consumer Goods Cloud TPM Accredited Professional Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This exam combines Salesforce configuration with consumer goods business concepts. Be ready to explain funds, tactics, baselines, sales lift, claims, and how each fits into the promotion cycle.
bullets: 62 scored questions in 75 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
66% to pass, which is 41 correct answers out of 62.
Business terms. Baseline volume, incremental volume, trade spend, ROI and deductions all come up.
The full cycle. Plan, fund, run, settle and review promotions.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice explaining a promotion from planning through settlement and review. Use practice questions to check your understanding of promotion ROI.

examFormat.heading: Consumer Goods Cloud TPM Accredited Professional Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Accredited Professional exams are taken online. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Questions commonly focus on a stage of the promotion cycle, such as setting a budget, planning a price reduction, or settling a retailer claim.
bestWayToPass: Trace a promotion: Follow account planning, tactics, funding, execution, claims, and the final review.
Review funding: Connect budgets and accruals with payments and claims for a promotion.
Compare volumes: Baseline volume estimates ordinary sales; incremental volume is the extra attributed to the promotion.
Know where data comes from: Shipments from the ERP and sell-out from retailer data.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you set up and use Consumer Goods Cloud Trade Promotion Management: account planning, promotions and tactics, funds, claims and settlement, and promotion analytics.

keyConcepts.h2: Consumer Goods TPM AP: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Trade Promotion Planning & Fund Management
blocks.body: Retailers and consumer goods companies use trade funds to pay for promotions. An account plan sets volume, revenue and spending goals. A fixed fund has a set budget; a variable fund can increase with sales. Track planned, committed and actual spending against the fund.

blocks.heading: Promotion Execution & Tactics
blocks.body: A promotion defines the retailer, products and dates. Its tactics describe activities such as a price reduction, display or flyer placement. Each tactic has an expected cost and sales effect. Teams can use approval rules and templates to manage promotion spending.

blocks.heading: Settlement & Claims Processing
blocks.body: A retailer may request payment through a claim or subtract an amount from an invoice as a deduction. Match the request to the promotion and tactic, check the amount, and investigate differences before approving payment. This helps prevent duplicate payment and inaccurate spend.

blocks.heading: Forecasting & Baseline Analytics
blocks.body: Baseline volume is the estimated sales without a promotion. Incremental volume is the additional sales attributed to it. Compare incremental profit with promotion costs to assess return, then compare forecast and actual results after the event.

blocks.heading: Integration with ERP & Retailer Data
blocks.body: TPM uses shipment and invoice data from ERP systems and point-of-sale data from retailers or providers. Product and account hierarchies support planning at the right level. Consistent customer and product IDs help connect transactions and send settlement information back to finance.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Consumer Goods Trade Promotion Management Accredited Professional Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Questions usually describe one step in the promotion cycle. Identify the record or measure that applies at that point.

blocks.heading: Trade Promotion Planning
blocks.body: Start with account targets for sales and spending, then connect the relevant promotion and tactics.

blocks.heading: Fund Management
blocks.body: Check whether the budget is fixed or grows with sales, and identify which fund the promotion uses.

blocks.heading: Account Planning
blocks.body: Compare the account plan with planned promotions to find gaps against targets.

blocks.heading: Promotion Settlement & Claims
blocks.body: Connect the claim or deduction to the correct activity and investigate any amount that differs from the agreement.

blocks.heading: Analytics for TPM
blocks.body: Use incremental sales when assessing a promotion, then compare the forecast with actual results.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer sold 12,000 cases during a promotion. Sales without the promotion were expected to be 9,000. How many cases were incremental?
options: 12,000 cases
3,000 cases
21,000 cases
9,000 cases
sampleQuestions.explanation: Incremental volume is the extra volume caused by the promotion: total minus baseline, so 12,000 minus 9,000.
whyWrong: 12,000 is total volume, which includes sales that would have happened anyway.
Adding them together has no meaning here.
9,000 is the baseline.

sampleQuestions.question: A brand sets aside five cents per shipped case for retailer promotions. Which fund type fits?
options: A variable fund that grows as eligible shipment volume increases
A deduction taken from the retailer invoice after a sale
A fixed fund with a balance agreed before the period starts
A retailer claim requesting payment for a promotion
sampleQuestions.explanation: The amount depends on how many cases are shipped, so the fund grows with volume.
whyWrong: A deduction is money the retailer takes off an invoice.
A fixed fund has a set amount decided in advance.
A claim is a retailer's request to be paid.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer uses both a temporary price cut and an in-store display during one two-week campaign. How should these be represented?
options: As separate promotions managed in different planning periods
As separate funds
As one activity split into two separate claim records
As two tactics in one promotion
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tactics describe the activities within a promotion, each with its own cost and effect.
whyWrong: Account plans cover the whole year for a retailer.
Funds pay for tactics, they don't describe them.
Claims come after the promotion.

sampleQuestions.question: After a promotion, a retailer reduces its next invoice by $8,000. What is this amount?
options: A deduction linked to the promotion and taken off an invoice
A tactic that describes one planned promotional activity
A sales baseline used to estimate expected volume without promotion
A fund that holds the budget available for promotional spending
sampleQuestions.explanation: Deductions are amounts the retailer takes off an invoice, which must be matched and checked against what was agreed.
whyWrong: A tactic is a planned activity.
Baseline is a volume measure.
A fund is a budget.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer submits a claim that is $2,000 above the agreed tactic cost. What should the team do?
options: Automatically increase the fund budget
Review the difference before approving payment
Delete the promotion
Pay the entire claim immediately
sampleQuestions.explanation: Differences should be checked before paying, so the company doesn't overpay.
whyWrong: Raising the budget hides the problem.
Deleting the promotion loses the record.
Paying without checking risks paying for things that weren't agreed.

sampleQuestions.question: Which measure best indicates whether a promotion delivered value for its cost?
options: Total units sold, including volume that may have occurred anyway
The number of tactics used to carry out the promotion
ROI comparing incremental profit with the cost of the promotion
The length of time the promotion remained active
sampleQuestions.explanation: ROI looks at the extra profit the promotion created against what it cost.
whyWrong: Total volume includes sales that would have happened anyway.
More tactics doesn't mean better results.
Length doesn't measure value.

sampleQuestions.question: Where does a company's shipment, or sell-in, data usually originate?
options: The fund record
The account plan
The retailer's promotional flyer
The company's ERP
sampleQuestions.explanation: Shipments and invoices are recorded in the ERP and loaded into TPM.
whyWrong: Funds hold budgets.
Account plans hold targets.
The flyer is a promotion activity.

sampleQuestions.question: Planners need to compare a promotion's actual results with its forecast. Which analysis should they use?
options: A fund transfer
Post-event analysis
A retailer claim
A new account plan
sampleQuestions.explanation: Post-event analysis compares forecast with actual results, which improves future planning.
whyWrong: A fund transfer moves budget.
A claim is a payment request.
An account plan sets targets for the future.

sampleQuestions.question: A key account manager needs to check whether planned promotions will meet a retailer's annual volume target. Which record should they review?
options: The retailer's account plan with its annual targets and planned activity
The product price used to calculate the retailer order value
An individual claim submitted after a promotion has ended
The ERP invoice list showing past shipments and customer charges
sampleQuestions.explanation: Account plans compare targets with planned promotions, showing gaps early.
whyWrong: Price alone doesn't show targets.
One claim shows one payment.
Invoices show past sales, not plans against targets.

sampleQuestions.question: A proposed promotion would spend more than the fund's remaining balance. What should happen?
options: Proceed without checking whether the planned spend fits the available budget
Delete the fund record so the promotion can be approved without a limit
Send the plan through approval rules before committing the promotion spend
Automatically approve the related claim before checking the fund balance
sampleQuestions.explanation: Approval rules can check spend against available funds before a promotion goes ahead.
whyWrong: Ignoring funds defeats budget control.
Deleting the fund loses budget tracking.
Automatic approval risks overspending.

sampleQuestions.question: A data provider sends weekly retailer point-of-sale data. What does this data help TPM measure?
options: The tactics planned for the promotion and retailer account
A replacement for the ERP
What consumers actually purchased
The budget assigned to each fund
sampleQuestions.explanation: Sell-out data shows real consumer purchases, which helps measure promotion effect.
whyWrong: Tactics are planned by users.
The ERP still holds shipments and invoices.
Budgets are set separately.

sampleQuestions.question: A team wants to plan retailer-group promotions at the brand level instead of for each item. What data structure supports this?
options: A separate Salesforce org for each brand and retailer group
Manual spreadsheets used to plan each brand and customer group
Product and account hierarchies
A separate fund for every item
sampleQuestions.explanation: Hierarchies let users plan at higher levels, like brand and retailer group, and roll numbers up and down.
whyWrong: A separate org isn't needed.
Spreadsheets bypass the system.
A fund per item is the opposite of planning at brand level.

sampleQuestions.question: Teams repeatedly create the same promotion type from scratch. What can make setup faster and more consistent?
options: Longer promotion periods
Fewer tactics
Additional funds
Promotion templates
sampleQuestions.explanation: Templates pre-fill common promotion types, so they are faster to create and set up the same way.
whyWrong: Length doesn't affect setup time.
Fewer tactics may not match the plan.
More funds don't speed up setup.

sampleQuestions.question: Why should product and customer identifiers align across TPM, the ERP, and retailer data?
options: To match shipment, sell-out, and claim records for the right products and customers
To lower the amount paid for promotional tactics across all retailers
To stop a fund from reaching its approved spending limit during the period
To improve the speed of pages on the company website for retail users
sampleQuestions.explanation: Consistent IDs let the system tie each piece of data to the right product, customer and promotion.
whyWrong: Costs are set by the tactic, not the ID.
Matching IDs doesn't add money to funds.
Website speed is unrelated.

sampleQuestions.question: A promotion increased sales volume, but its deep price cut reduced profit. What does this result show?
options: Any promotion that raises sales is profitable
A large volume lift does not guarantee a positive ROI
Baselines are irrelevant
The fund balance was too small
sampleQuestions.explanation: ROI depends on profit, not just volume. A deep discount can drive volume while losing money.
whyWrong: Lift and profit are not the same thing.
Baselines are needed to measure lift.
Fund size doesn't explain lost profit.
